title: The oldest known art
description: The oldest reliably dated cave art is a hand stencil on Muna island, Indonesia, at least 67,800 years old; art is far older than writing.

facts.text: A hand stencil in Liang Metanduno cave on Muna island, Indonesia, is at least 67,800 years old, the oldest reliably dated cave art yet found.
A hand stencil is made by pressing a hand to the rock and blowing or spraying pigment such as red ochre over it, so the hand's outline stays on bare rock.
Writing (Sumerian cuneiform) emerged around the end of the 4th millennium BCE, about 5,200 years ago.
Leonardo da Vinci began painting the Mona Lisa about 1503.

Squeezing the 67,800 years since the oldest known cave art into one 24-hour day, writing (about 5,200 years ago) appears just after 10 p.m., after more than 22 hours, and the Mona Lisa (about 1503) about 11 minutes before midnight.

title: The big eras of art
description: Western art history is told as a run of eras (Stone Age, ancient, medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, modern), each partly answering the one before.

facts.text: Britannica's history of Western painting runs from the Stone Age through ancient Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Baroque and the Neoclassical and Romantic periods to modern art.
Prehistoric art includes paintings on cave walls, like those at Chauvet and Lascaux, and small portable carvings in bone and ivory.
Ancient Egyptian art, made over about three thousand years BCE, served the king and the gods.
From late antiquity to the Counter-Reformation, Western art was essentially the art of the church.
Renaissance is French for 'rebirth'; beginning in 14th-century Italy, it revived the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome.
Baroque art, roughly of the 1600s, aimed for drama, movement and emotion.
Modern painting began in mid-19th-century France and rejected traditional rules; photography freed painting from being the only way to depict the world accurately.

title: Bird in Space on trial
description: In 1926 US customs taxed Brancusi's Bird in Space as metal because it did not look like a bird; in 1928 a court ruled it a work of art.

facts.text: In 1926 US customs refused to accept Constantin Brancusi's bronze Bird in Space as a sculpture and charged a 40% duty on it as a manufacture of metal.
In Bird in Space, Brancusi left out wings and feathers, elongated the body and reduced the head and beak to a slanted oval; the bronze is polished like a mirror.
Bird in Space conveys the idea of flight rather than the look of a particular bird.
In 1928 a US customs court ruled Bird in Space an original sculpture and a work of art, recognizing a new school of art that portrays abstract ideas rather than imitating natural objects.
The court admitted it might be hard to associate the sculpture with a bird, but found it pleasing to look at.

title: What counts as art?
description: People have disagreed over whether art must imitate nature or may express ideas; the Brancusi case shows the old and new definitions colliding.

facts.text: Before the Brancusi case, US courts treated sculpture as work carved or shaped in the likeness of natural models, such as people and animals.
At the trial, critic Frank Crowninshield testified that the work suggested flight, grace and speed, just as a bird does.

title: The elements of art
description: The building blocks of any artwork: line, shape, color, texture and space (many lists add form).

facts.text: The elements of art are the building blocks artists use to make a work of art: line, shape, form, space, color and texture.
A line is a mark longer than it is wide; lines can be straight or curved, thick or thin.
A shape is a closed line; shapes are flat and can be geometric, like squares and circles, or organic, like free-form natural shapes.
In art, color is light reflected off objects.
Texture is the surface quality of a work, real or implied; a drawing of a porcupine may look prickly, but the paper is still smooth.
Form means three-dimensional shapes, such as balls, cylinders and boxes.

title: Space and negative space
description: Space is the area around and between things; the empty part, negative space, has a shape too. Space also means the feeling of depth.

facts.text: Space is the area around and between objects; the empty space around them is negative space, which has a shape too. Space can also mean the feeling of depth.

title: The color wheel and primary colors
description: Newton bent the spectrum into a circle; painters' primaries are red, yellow and blue, and mixing two gives a secondary color.

facts.text: In Opticks (1704), Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early color wheel.
In traditional color theory for painters, the primary colors are red, yellow and blue; other colors are mixes of them.
Mixing two primary colors makes a secondary color: orange, green or violet.

title: Complementary colors
description: Complements sit opposite on the color wheel; side by side they make each other look more intense (Chevreul's simultaneous contrast), mixed they make brown.

facts.text: Complementary colors sit directly across the color wheel, such as red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and violet; each pair shares no common primary.
Mixed together, complementary paints neutralize each other and make brown.
Soon after becoming director of dyeing at the Gobelins royal tapestry works in Paris in 1824, chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul received complaints that the tapestry colors looked weak.
Chevreul found the problem was optical, not the dye: colors placed side by side change how each other look. He published this law of simultaneous contrast in 1839.
Complementary colors placed side by side make each other look more intense.
Chevreul's color ideas influenced painters, including the Impressionists.

title: The oldest known drawing
description: A crosshatch drawn in red ochre on a stone flake at Blombos Cave, South Africa, about 73,000 years old; whether it is art is debated.

facts.text: A crosshatch drawn with a red ochre crayon on a stone flake from Blombos Cave, South Africa, is about 73,000 years old, the oldest known drawing.
The Blombos drawing is at least 30,000 years older than other known abstract and figurative drawings.
Researchers debate whether the Blombos lines were meant as art; they may instead be left over from sharpening the ochre crayon.
Cave artists made reds from iron oxides such as hematite (red ochre) and blacks from manganese dioxide and charcoal.

title: Hand stencils
description: How hand stencils were made by blowing pigment around a hand, and how the Muna stencil's fingers were narrowed into a claw.

facts.text: Someone later narrowed the fingers of the Muna hand stencil, making it look like a claw.
Cave artists sometimes blew pigment onto the wall through a pipe.

title: The oldest picture story
description: A scene of three human-like figures and a wild pig at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, at least 51,200 years old, dated from mineral crusts over the paint.

facts.text: A cave painting at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, showing three human-like figures interacting with a wild pig, is at least 51,200 years old, the oldest known narrative art.
The Leang Karampuang scene was dated by uranium-series analysis of thin calcium carbonate crusts that formed on top of the paint.

title: Lascaux
description: The Lascaux cave paintings in France: found in 1940, about 17,000 years old, the Hall of the Bulls, and closed in 1963 after visitors damaged them.

facts.text: Lascaux cave in France was discovered by four teenagers in September 1940.
Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from Lascaux gives a date of about 17,000 years ago.
Lascaux's Hall of the Bulls holds four huge black bulls, or aurochs, some about 5 meters long, with their horns shown in 'twisted perspective'.
Lascaux's painters used scaffolding to reach high walls and the ceiling.
Lascaux opened to the public in 1948; up to 100,000 visitors a year and artificial lighting faded its colors and brought algae, bacteria and crystals, so it closed in 1963.
A partial replica, Lascaux II, opened nearby in 1983.
Lascaux's paintings lasted about 17,000 years in the dark, then about 15 years of public visits (1948 to 1963) damaged them.

title: Chauvet
description: Chauvet Cave in France: about 35,500 years old, full of dangerous animals, drawn with scraped walls, strong outlines and shading.

facts.text: In 1994, explorers found Chauvet Cave in southern France after feeling a faint draft from a heap of stones.
Rockfalls blocked Chauvet Cave's entrance, and the last one sealed it at least 21,000 years ago, until explorers found it in 1994.
Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and drawings shows most of Chauvet's art is about 35,500 years old, roughly twice Lascaux's age.
Chauvet holds over 400 images of animals from 14 species, with many dangerous ones: cave lions, woolly rhinos, mammoths and bears.
Chauvet's artists scraped walls to make a blank surface, strengthened outlines to make figures stand out and used stump drawing (smudging) for shading.
In Chauvet's End Chamber, lions are shown hunting bison.

title: The Lion-Man
description: A mammoth-ivory figure with a lion's head and upright human body, about 40,000 years old, from Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany.

facts.text: The Lion-Man, carved from mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, has a cave lion's head on an upright, partly human body.
The Lion-Man was found in Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany; it is 31 cm tall, the largest known sculpture of Ice Age art.
Carving a copy of the Lion-Man with Ice Age-style stone tools took an experimenter hundreds of hours.

title: Ice Age figures of women
description: Small Ice Age carvings of women such as the Venus of Hohle Fels and the Venus of Willendorf, and why their meaning and name are uncertain.

facts.text: The Venus of Hohle Fels, from a German cave, is a 6 cm mammoth-ivory figure of a woman, 35,000 to 40,000 years old, with a pierced loop instead of a head, so it may have been worn as a pendant.
The Venus of Willendorf, found in Austria in 1908, is an 11.1 cm limestone figure of a woman tinted with red ochre, about 30,000 years old, with no face, only a pattern like a braid or cap.
The name 'Venus', after the Roman goddess of love, was given by modern scholars; the figures were carved many thousands of years before Rome.
Ideas about the Venus of Willendorf include a fertility figure, a good-luck charm and a mother goddess.
A 2022 study found the Venus of Willendorf's stone likely came from the Lake Garda region of northern Italy, across the Alps.

title: Stonehenge
description: How Stonehenge was built: dates, where the stones came from, the woodworking joints and the hundreds of people needed.

facts.text: Stonehenge began as a circular ditch and bank about 3000 BC; its stones were set up about 2500 BC, roughly 4,500 years ago.
Stonehenge's sarsens, about 25 tons on average, came from West Woods about 25 km away; its bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 km away.
Stonehenge's lintels were fitted with mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints, usually found only in woodworking.
Building the stone circle needed hundreds of people to move, shape and raise the stones.

title: Gatherings at Stonehenge
description: Stonehenge's solstice alignment and the midwinter feasts at Durrington Walls, with animals brought from across Britain.

facts.text: Stonehenge is aligned with the Sun: at midsummer the sun rises beside the Heel Stone, and at midwinter it originally set between the uprights of the tallest trilithon.

At Durrington Walls near Stonehenge, over 38,000 animal bones have been found; pig teeth show animals raised as far away as west Wales, northern England and north-east Scotland, slaughtered at midwinter for feasts.

title: Göbekli Tepe
description: Carved T-shaped stone pillars built by hunter-gatherers about 11,500 years ago, before farming.

facts.text: Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey was built by hunter-gatherers, before farming, beginning about 11,500 years ago: more than twice Stonehenge's age.
Göbekli Tepe's T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters tall and weigh up to 50 tons; some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions.
Some Göbekli Tepe pillars have carved arms and hands meeting across the front, and belts; researchers read the T-pillars as larger-than-life stylized people.
Göbekli Tepe suggests that building together may have led people to settle, rather than following settlement.

title: Art to record the world
description: Ideas that early art came from a basic urge to record the world, or served as records such as counts and seasonal calendars.

facts.text: The exact purpose of prehistoric art is still debated.
One view sees Paleolithic art as coming from a basic human need to creatively record and recreate the world around us.
Some researchers suggest Paleolithic animal images showing seasonal coats may be an early seasonal notation system.
Researchers suggest the patterns on an engraved ochre plaque from Blombos Cave may be a way of counting or storing information.

title: The hunting magic idea
description: The idea that animal images were magic for successful hunts, and the Lascaux reindeer problem.

facts.text: Some scholars see prehistoric animal images as magic to make hunting succeed or to guarantee fertility.
Reindeer were the Lascaux artists' main food, yet reindeer are almost absent from Lascaux's walls.

title: The spirit world idea
description: The idea that cave art was symbolic or religious, perhaps tied to shamans and part-human, part-animal beings.

facts.text: Cave art is generally thought to have had a symbolic or religious function, sometimes both.
Some experts think cave art was made within shamanic beliefs, in which a shaman enters a trance to contact spirits.
Researchers suggest the Muna stencil's claw-like fingers may reflect links between people and animals, or spiritual beliefs.

title: How cave art is dated
description: Radiocarbon dates once-living material like charcoal; uranium-series dates mineral crusts over paint, giving a minimum age.

facts.text: Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in once-living material such as charcoal, and works for specimens up to about 50,000 years old.
Many cave paintings use mineral pigments with no organic material, so radiocarbon cannot date them.
Uranium-series dating of mineral crusts that formed on top of a painting gives a minimum age: the paint underneath must be older.
